los.text: Describe the clinical features of asthma and how these affect a patient’s daily life.
los.html:
AsthmaChronic inflammatory airway disease with variable symptoms and variable, reversible airflow obstruction and bronchial hyperresponsiveness.
Symptoms
  • Wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness, cough (often nocturnal/early morning)
  • Variable over time and intensity
  • Triggers: viral infections, allergens (house dust mite, pollen, pets), exercise, cold air, smoke, pollution, NSAIDs/β-blockers, stress, occupational agents (improves on days off/holidays).
Supporting historyAtopy (eczema, hay fever), FHx asthma/atopy, childhood onset.
SignsOften normal between attacks; polyphonic expiratory wheeze; hyperinflation in chronic severe; nasal polyps (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease).
Impact on daily life
  • Night waking/sleep disturbance
  • Exercise limitation
  • Time off school/work
  • Emergency attendances and admissions
  • Anxiety and fear of attacks
  • Side effects of treatment (oral steroids)
  • Stigma using inhalers
  • Cost of prescriptions (free in Wales)
  • Restrictions on activities/careers
  • Family disruption
  • and risk of death (~1,200/year UK; many preventable: NRAD report).
Assess controlSymptom frequency, reliever use (>3×/week = poor), night waking, activity limitation, exacerbations/oral steroid courses; validated tools (ACT, RCP 3 questions).

los.text: Describe the main investigations used in the diagnosis and monitoring of asthma.
los.html:
Objective tests support diagnosis (BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024 joint guideline).
Adults (≥17)
  • (1) blood eosinophil count (above reference range) or FeNO ≥50 ppb → diagnose.
  • (2) Otherwise spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility (BDR): FEV1 ↑ ≥12% and ≥200 mL (or ≥10% of predicted) → diagnose.
  • (3) Otherwise peak flow variability >20% over 2 weeks.
  • (4) Otherwise refer for bronchial challenge (methacholine/mannitol).
Children 5–16FeNO ≥35 ppb → then BDR → then PEF variability → then skin prick/IgE to house dust mite/eosinophils, referral.
Under 5sDiagnosis based on clinical judgement; treat as suspected asthma and review.
SpirometryObstructive pattern FEV1/FVC <0.7 (or below LLN); may be normal between episodes.
OtherCXR (exclude alternatives, not routine), allergy testing (skin prick, specific IgE), occupational PEF monitoring (serial work/rest), FBC.
MonitoringSymptom scores (ACT), PEF diary, spirometry, FeNO (adherence/inflammation), exacerbation history, inhaler technique, personalised asthma action plan review; annual review.

los.text: Describe the principles of management of asthma, including reliever and preventer therapies
los.html:
Principles
  • Anti-inflammatory therapy (ICS) for everyone
  • Avoid SABA-only treatment in ≥12s (SABA overuse is linked to deaths)
  • Check adherence, inhaler technique, triggers before stepping up
  • Step down when controlled ≥3 months.
RelieversSABA (salbutamol) or, now preferred in ≥12s, as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol (AIR therapy).
PreventersInhaled corticosteroids (beclometasone, budesonide, fluticasone) ± LABA (formoterol, salmeterol; never without ICS), LTRA (montelukast), LAMA (tiotropium), biologics.
BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024 pathway (≥12 years)
1. AIRAs-needed low-dose budesonide/formoterol.
2Low-dose MART (maintenance and reliever therapy with ICS/formoterol).
3Moderate-dose MART.
4Check FeNO/eosinophils: if raised → refer specialist; if not → add LTRA or LAMA (trial 8–12 weeks).
5. SpecialistHigh-dose ICS, biologics (anti-IL-5 mepolizumab/benralizumab, anti-IgE omalizumab, anti-TSLP tezepelumab), oral steroids.
Children 5–11Paediatric low-dose ICS + SABA → add LTRA or switch to paediatric low-dose MART → moderate-dose → refer.
Non-drugSmoking cessation, trigger avoidance, weight loss, breathing exercises, vaccinations (influenza, COVID), written personalised action plan, self-management education.

los.text: Develop literature review skills in relation to specific healthcare issues
sessions: MHS: Critical Appraisal 2: Randomised control trials
los.html:
Randomised controlled trials (RCTs)Participants randomly allocated to intervention or control → balances known and unknown confounders; gold standard for evaluating interventions.
Key features to appraise (CASP RCT / CONSORT)
  • Clearly focused question (PICO).
  • Randomisation (method: computer-generated) and allocation concealment (prevents selection bias).
  • Blinding (participants, clinicians, outcome assessors; double-blind) to reduce performance/detection bias.
  • Groups similar at baseline (Table 1).
  • Groups treated equally apart from intervention.
  • Follow-up complete, losses accounted for; intention-to-treat analysis (analyse as randomised: preserves randomisation; per-protocol overestimates).
  • Sample size/power calculation; primary outcome pre-specified (trial registration).
  • Results: effect size with 95% CI, p-values, RRR, ARR, NNT (=1/ARR), harms.
  • Applicability: similar patients? all important outcomes considered? benefits worth harms and costs?
Bias typesSelection, performance, detection, attrition, reporting (selective outcome), publication bias. Cochrane Risk of Bias (RoB 2) tool.
LimitationsExpensive, ethical constraints, short follow-up, strict inclusion criteria (limited generalisability/external validity), rare harms missed.
VariantsCrossover, cluster, factorial, pragmatic vs explanatory, non-inferiority trials.

los.text: Describe the common causes of wheeze in childhood at different ages and outline basic principles of management
los.html:
AgeCommon causes
Infants (<1–2 yrs)
  • Bronchiolitis (RSV; peak <6 months; coryza → cough, wheeze, crackles, poor feeding; supportive: O₂, NG/IV fluids)
  • Congenital (tracheomalacia, vascular ring, CF, BPD in ex-preterms)
  • GORD/aspiration
  • Cow's milk allergy
  • Heart failure (VSD)
Preschool (1–5 yrs)
  • Viral-induced (episodic) wheeze (only with colds, no interval symptoms; most outgrow)
  • Multiple-trigger wheeze (between colds too; more likely to become asthma)
  • Inhaled foreign body (sudden onset, unilateral/monophonic wheeze, choking episode → bronchoscopy)
  • Croup (stridor, not wheeze)
School-ageAsthma (commonest), viral LRTI, foreign body, CF, PCD, bronchiectasis, dysfunctional breathing, anaphylaxis
Red flagsWheeze from birth, faltering growth, chronic wet cough/sputum, focal signs, clubbing, persistent hypoxia, sudden onset/choking → investigate (CXR, sweat test, bronchoscopy).
Management principles
  • Acute wheeze: assess severity (RR, work of breathing, sats, ability to talk/feed), salbutamol via spacer (± nebulised with O₂ if severe), ipratropium, oral prednisolone (asthma/multiple trigger; not routinely for viral wheeze), O₂ for sats <92%, IV magnesium/salbutamol/aminophylline if severe, HDU/PICU.
  • Bronchiolitis: supportive only (no bronchodilators/steroids/antibiotics).
  • Preschool viral wheeze: SABA via spacer; consider LTRA (montelukast) or ICS trial if frequent/severe.
  • Asthma: as LO 3 (paediatric pathway); spacer technique, action plans, school plans, reduce smoke exposure.

los.text: Explain the underlying pathophysiology of asthma and how it relates to clinical signs and symptoms.
los.html:
Inflammation
  • Atopic susceptibility → allergen sensitisation → Th2 response (IL-4 → IgE class switching; IL-5 → eosinophils; IL-13 → mucus, hyperresponsiveness)
  • ILC2 cells
  • Epithelial alarmins (TSLP, IL-33, IL-25) from damaged epithelium.
  • Non-allergic/neutrophilic (Th17) phenotypes in some (obesity, smoking).
Early phase (minutes)
  • Allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells → histamine, cysteinyl leukotrienes, PGD2 → bronchial smooth muscle contraction, oedema, mucus → acute wheeze/breathlessness
  • Reverses with SABA.
Late phase (4–8 h)Recruitment of eosinophils, Th2 cells, basophils → sustained inflammation, hyperresponsiveness → nocturnal symptoms; prevented by ICS.
Airway hyperresponsivenessExaggerated narrowing to triggers (cold air, exercise, irritants).
Airway remodelling(chronic)Subepithelial fibrosis (basement membrane thickening), smooth muscle hypertrophy/hyperplasia, goblet cell hyperplasia, mucous gland enlargement, angiogenesis → fixed obstruction in some.
Link to clinical features
  • Bronchoconstriction + oedema + mucus plugs
  • → ↓ airway radius (resistance ∝ 1/r⁴)
  • → expiratory wheeze (turbulent flow through narrowed airways), prolonged expiration, air trapping/hyperinflation, ↑ work of breathing, V/Q mismatch → hypoxaemia
  • Early hyperventilation → low PaCO₂
  • Normal/rising PaCO₂ in acute asthma = exhaustion (life-threatening)
  • "silent chest" = minimal airflow.
  • Diurnal variation (circadian ↓ cortisol/adrenaline, ↑ vagal tone at night).

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of drugs used to treat asthma and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients.
los.html:
DrugMechanismKey points
SABA (salbutamol)β2 agonist → Gs → ↑ cAMP → PKA → smooth muscle relaxation
  • Rapid (minutes), 4–6 h.
  • SE: tremor, tachycardia, palpitations, hypokalaemia, lactic acidosis (high dose).
  • Overuse (>2–3 canisters/yr) = poor control, ↑ death risk
ICS (beclometasone, budesonide, fluticasone)Glucocorticoid receptor → ↓ inflammatory gene transcription (cytokines), ↑ β2 receptor expression, ↓ eosinophils
  • Cornerstone
  • ↓ exacerbations and deaths.
  • SE: oral candidiasis, dysphonia (rinse mouth, spacer)
  • High dose: adrenal suppression, growth slowing in children, bone loss, cataracts
LABA (formoterol (fast onset), salmeterol (slow))Long-acting β2 agonists (12 h)Never as monotherapy (↑ deaths: SMART trial) → always with ICS. Formoterol suits MART/AIR
ICS/formoterol (Symbicort, Fostair)CombinationAIR/MART: ↓ severe exacerbations vs SABA reliever (SYGMA, Novel START trials)
LTRA (montelukast)CysLT1 receptor antagonistAdd-on, exercise-induced, aspirin-sensitive, preschool wheeze. SE: neuropsychiatric (nightmares, mood: MHRA warning)
LAMA (tiotropium)M3 antagonistAdd-on in adults; dry mouth
TheophyllinePDE inhibition, adenosine antagonismNarrow therapeutic index; CYP450 interactions (↑ with clarithromycin, ciprofloxacin; ↓ with smoking); arrhythmias, seizures
Oral prednisoloneSystemic steroidExacerbations (adults 40–50 mg ≥5 days); maintenance in severe
BiologicsOmalizumab (anti-IgE), mepolizumab/reslizumab (anti-IL-5), benralizumab (anti-IL-5R), dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα), tezepelumab (anti-TSLP)Severe eosinophilic/allergic asthma; ↓ exacerbations and steroid use
Acute severe asthma
  • O₂ (target 93–95%)
  • Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg (back-to-back if needed)
  • Ipratropium 500 μg
  • Prednisolone 40–50 mg or IV hydrocortisone 100 mg
  • IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 min
  • IV aminophylline/salbutamol (senior)
  • ICU if life-threatening.
Delivery
  • pMDI + spacer (best for children and acute), DPI (needs fast inspiratory flow), breath-actuated
  • Inhaler technique check every review
  • Greener options (DPIs have lower carbon footprint).

los.text: Discuss clinical signs and symptoms of asthma and the impact of this condition on a patient's life.
los.html:
SymptomsEpisodic wheeze, cough (night/early morning), breathlessness, chest tightness; triggered by viruses, allergens, exercise, cold, smoke; variable; better with bronchodilator.
Signs between attacksOften none; during exacerbations: tachypnoea, wheeze, prolonged expiration, accessory muscles, inability to complete sentences.
Acute asthma severity (adults, BTS)Features
ModeratePEF 50–75% best/predicted, no severe features
Acute severePEF 33–50%, RR ≥25, HR ≥110, can't complete sentences
Life-threateningPEF <33%, SpO₂ <92%, PaO₂ <8 kPa, normal PaCO₂ (4.6–6.0), silent chest, cyanosis, poor respiratory effort, arrhythmia, exhaustion, altered consciousness, hypotension
Near-fatalRaised PaCO₂ and/or need for mechanical ventilation
Impact on life(see LO 1)
  • Sleep, school/work, sport, psychological (anxiety, embarrassment), family, finances, risk of severe attacks and death
  • Children: growth, missed school, parental anxiety.
  • Good control should allow a normal life.
Risk factors for fatal/near-fatal asthmaPrevious near-fatal attack/ICU, ≥3 classes of medication, heavy SABA use, frequent ED attendances, poor adherence, psychosocial problems (depression, alcohol, denial), non-attendance.

los.text: Explain the general approach to assessing a patient with suspected asthma, including key features in the history and examination.
los.html:
History
  • Symptoms: wheeze, cough, breathlessness, chest tightness; variability (diurnal, seasonal), triggers, nocturnal symptoms, exercise.
  • Onset (childhood?), previous episodes, response to treatment (inhalers, steroids), exacerbations, admissions, ICU.
  • Atopy: eczema, allergic rhinitis, food allergy; FHx asthma/atopy.
  • Occupational history (better on days off/holidays? exposures: isocyanates (paint sprayers), flour (bakers), latex, wood dust), pets, home environment (damp, mould).
  • Drugs: β-blockers (including eye drops), NSAIDs/aspirin.
  • Smoking/vaping, second-hand smoke.
  • Red flags/alternatives: weight loss, haemoptysis, chronic sputum, smoking history >20 pack-years (COPD), cardiac symptoms, voice change/stridor (upper airway), dysfunctional breathing.
Examination
  • General (respiratory distress, accessory muscles), hands (clubbing: not asthma → think CF/bronchiectasis/cancer), polyphonic expiratory wheeze, hyperinflation, nasal polyps, eczema
  • Often normal.
  • PEF measurement.
ThenObjective testing (FeNO/eosinophils, spirometry with BDR, PEF variability), consider differentials, treat and review response.

los.text: Assess the quality of the analyses performed in published research papers and the relevance of those findings in practice.
los.html:
Assessing the quality of analyses
  • Appropriate statistical tests for data type and distribution: parametric (t-test, ANOVA: normal continuous data) vs non-parametric (Mann–Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal–Wallis); chi-squared/Fisher's for categorical; correlation/regression for associations (linear, logistic, Cox for survival/time-to-event).
  • Pre-specified primary outcome and analysis plan; beware multiple comparisons/subgroup fishing (false positives), p-hacking, outcome switching.
  • Statistical vs clinical significance: p <0.05 (probability of results at least this extreme if null true) doesn't mean important; look at effect size and 95% CI (precision; CI crossing 1 for ratios/0 for differences = not significant).
  • Type I error (α; false positive) vs type II (β; false negative; low power), power (1−β; typically 80–90%) from sample size calculation.
  • Confounding adjustment (multivariable models), missing data handling (imputation), intention-to-treat.
  • Appropriate summary measures: RR, OR, HR, ARR, NNT/NNH, mean difference.
  • Diagnostic studies: sensitivity, specificity, PPV/NPV (depend on prevalence), likelihood ratios, ROC curves.
Relevance in practiceAre participants like my patients? patient-important outcomes (mortality vs surrogate)? absolute benefit worthwhile vs harms and costs? consistent with other evidence (systematic reviews)? feasible in local setting?
Hierarchy and reporting standardsCONSORT (RCTs), STROBE (observational), PRISMA (systematic reviews), STARD (diagnostic).

los.text: Systematically interpret an ECG using a structured, step-by-step method to identify normal and abnormal patterns.
los.html:
• Structured approach:
1Patient details, date/time, calibration (10 mm/mV) and paper speed (25 mm/s), compare with old ECGs.
2. Rate300 ÷ large squares between R waves (regular) or QRS count in 10 s strip × 6 (irregular). Normal 60–100.
3. RhythmRegular/irregular; P wave before every QRS? QRS after every P? (sinus rhythm).
4. AxisLeads I and aVF (both positive = normal; I positive, aVF negative → check II: negative = left axis deviation; I negative, aVF positive = right axis deviation).
5. P wavesPresent, morphology (P mitrale: bifid >0.12 s; P pulmonale: peaked >2.5 mm in II).
6. PR interval0.12–0.20 s (prolonged = 1st degree block; short = WPW).
7. QRS
  • Width (<0.12 s)
  • Q waves (pathological >1 small square wide or >25% of R)
  • R wave progression (V1→V6)
  • Voltage (LVH: S in V1 + R in V5/6 >35 mm).
8. ST segmentElevation/depression (measure at J point).
9. T wavesInversion (normal in aVR, V1, sometimes III), peaked (↑K⁺), flattened (↓K⁺).
10QT/QTc (Bazett: QT/√RR; prolonged >440 ms men/>460 women).
11Other: U waves (↓K⁺), delta waves, pacing spikes.
  • Summary: "This is a 12-lead ECG of ... showing sinus rhythm at 75 bpm, normal axis... In summary: ..."

los.text: Recognise ECG features of myocardial infarction, ischaemia, and common arrhythmias including heart blocks and atrial fibrillation/flutter.
los.html:
ConditionECG features
STEMI
  • ST elevation ≥1 mm in ≥2 contiguous limb leads or ≥2 mm in contiguous chest leads (thresholds vary by sex/age)
  • Reciprocal ST depression
  • Hyperacute T waves
  • Later pathological Q waves, T inversion.
  • New LBBB with symptoms.
  • Posterior MI: ST depression + tall R in V1–V3
TerritoriesInferior II, III, aVF (RCA); anterior/septal V1–V4 (LAD); lateral I, aVL, V5–V6 (circumflex); posterior V7–V9
NSTEMI/ischaemiaST depression (horizontal/downsloping), T wave inversion, or normal (troponin decides)
1st degree AV blockPR >0.2 s, every P conducted
Mobitz I (Wenckebach)Progressive PR lengthening until a P wave isn't conducted
Mobitz IIConstant PR with intermittent dropped QRS (risk of CHB → pacing)
3rd degree (complete) blockAV dissociation: P and QRS independent; slow escape rhythm (broad if ventricular)
Atrial fibrillationIrregularly irregular, no P waves, fibrillatory baseline; narrow QRS (unless aberrancy)
Atrial flutterSawtooth flutter waves (~300/min) in II, III, aVF, V1; usually 2:1 block → ventricular rate ~150 (regular)
SVTRegular narrow complex tachycardia 150–250, P waves hidden/retrograde
VTBroad complex (>120 ms) regular tachycardia, AV dissociation, capture/fusion beats
Bundle branch blocksQRS ≥120 ms; RBBB: RSR′ V1 (MaRRoW); LBBB: broad notched R in V6, deep S in V1 (WiLLiaM)
HyperkalaemiaPeaked T waves → flat P, wide QRS → sine wave
PericarditisWidespread saddle-shaped ST elevation + PR depression

los.text: Perform a systematic and competent respiratory examination.
los.html:
IntroductionWash hands, introduce, confirm identity, explain, consent, expose chest appropriately, position at 45°, ask about pain, chaperone if needed.
General inspection(end of bed)
  • Breathlessness, respiratory rate, accessory muscle use, pursed lips, cyanosis, cachexia, audible wheeze/stridor
  • Around bed: O₂, inhalers, nebulisers, sputum pot, peak flow meter, cigarettes.
Hands
  • Clubbing, tar staining, peripheral cyanosis, asterixis (CO₂ retention flap), fine tremor (β-agonist), wasting of small muscles (Pancoast)
  • Pulse (rate, rhythm, bounding in CO₂ retention), respiratory rate.
Face/neckCentral cyanosis (tongue), conjunctival pallor, Horner's syndrome, JVP, trachea position, lymph nodes (cervical, supraclavicular; sitting forward from behind), cricosternal distance.
Chest (anterior then posterior)
  • Inspection: shape (barrel, pectus), scars (thoracotomy, drains), symmetry of movement, deformity.
  • Palpation: chest expansion (upper and lower, front and back), apex beat, tactile vocal fremitus (optional).
  • Percussion: compare side to side (supraclavicular, clavicles, chest wall, axillae).
  • Auscultation: diaphragm, side to side, including axillae: breath sounds (vesicular/bronchial/reduced), added sounds (wheeze, crackles (fine/coarse), pleural rub), vocal resonance.
CompletePeripheral oedema, sacral oedema, calf (DVT). "To complete my examination I would: check observations including sats, PEF/spirometry, CXR, ABG, sputum sample".

los.text: Clearly and concisely describe relevant clinical findings from a respiratory examination using appropriate terminology and structure.
los.html:
Structure"I examined [name], a [age]-year-old [man/woman], who was comfortable at rest / breathless at rest on [x] L O₂..."
GeneralRespiratory rate, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis, surroundings (inhalers, O₂, sputum pot).
PeripheralClubbing, tar staining, flap, pulse, JVP, lymphadenopathy, trachea central/deviated.
Chest
  • Shape
  • Scars
  • Expansion (symmetrical/reduced on left)
  • Percussion (resonant/dull/stony dull/hyper-resonant)
  • Breath sounds (vesicular/bronchial/reduced)
  • Added sounds (fine end-inspiratory crackles at bases, polyphonic expiratory wheeze, coarse crackles)
  • Vocal resonance.
SummaryKey positive and relevant negative findings + most likely diagnosis + differentials + plan.
Example
  • "Mr X has signs of a right-sided pleural effusion: reduced expansion, stony dull percussion, reduced breath sounds and vocal resonance at the right base, trachea central.
  • Differentials include ...
  • I would like to perform a CXR and pleural USS..."
Pattern table
FindingExpansionPercussionBreath soundsVocal resonanceTrachea
Consolidation↓DullBronchial, crackles↑Central
Effusion↓Stony dull↓/absent↓Away (if large)
Pneumothorax↓Hyper-resonant↓/absent↓Away (tension)
Collapse↓Dull↓↓Towards
Fibrosis↓Normal/dullFine end-inspiratory cracklesNormal/↑Central (towards if upper lobe)
COPD/asthma↓ bilaterallyHyper-resonantWheeze, prolonged expirationNormalCentral

los.text: Apply clinical reasoning to examination findings to generate differential diagnoses and propose appropriate further investigations.
los.html:
• Integrate: history + examination pattern (ICM Year 2 › Respiratory › LO 2) → differential diagnoses → targeted investigations.
Clinical pictureLikely diagnosisNext investigations
Fever, productive cough, focal bronchial breathing/cracklesPneumoniaCXR, bloods (FBC, CRP, U&E: CURB-65), blood/sputum cultures, sats/ABG
Stony dull basePleural effusionCXR, pleural USS, diagnostic tap (Light's), CT if exudate/malignancy
Sudden breathlessness, hyper-resonancePneumothoraxErect CXR (unless tension: decompress first)
Bilateral fine end-inspiratory crackles, clubbingPulmonary fibrosis (ILD)HRCT, full PFTs (restrictive, ↓ TLCO), autoimmune screen
Wheeze, hyperinflation, smokerCOPDSpirometry (post-BD FEV1/FVC <0.7), CXR, FBC, α1-AT if young
Variable wheeze, atopyAsthmaFeNO/eosinophils, spirometry + BDR, PEF diary
Bibasal crackles, ↑ JVP, oedemaHeart failureCXR, ECG, NT-proBNP, echo
Clubbing, coarse crackles, chronic sputumBronchiectasisHRCT, sputum culture, immunoglobulins, CF testing
Weight loss, haemoptysis, clubbing, smokerLung cancerCXR → CT chest/abdomen, bronchoscopy/biopsy
Pleuritic pain, tachycardia, normal chestPEWells, D-dimer/CTPA

los.text: Demonstrate the correct use of a Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR) meter and spirometer, following appropriate technique and safety measures.
los.html:
PEFR
  • Set the meter to zero; patient standing (or sitting upright).
  • Deep breath in to total lung capacity, seal lips around mouthpiece, blow out as hard and fast as possible (short sharp "huff"; ≤1–2 s).
  • Best of 3 attempts (within 20 L/min); record in diary and compare with predicted (age, height, sex) or personal best; use correct scale (EU EN13826).
Spirometry(per ARTP standards)
  • Check contraindications (recent MI, pneumothorax, eye/abdominal surgery, haemoptysis), withhold bronchodilators before test (SABA 4–6 h, LABA 12–24 h) if testing reversibility.
  • Record age, height, sex, ethnicity; nose clip; sitting upright; disposable filter mouthpiece (infection control).
  • Relaxed (slow) VC then forced manoeuvre: maximal inhalation → tight seal → blast out as hard and fast as possible → keep going until no more air (≥6 s, plateau) → maximal inhalation.
  • At least 3 acceptable and repeatable blows (FEV1 and FVC within 150 mL); maximum ~8 attempts.
  • Reversibility: repeat 15–20 min after salbutamol 400 μg via spacer.
  • Watch for coughing, early termination, leak, submaximal effort; observe for dizziness/syncope.
SafetyInfection control, calibration/verification of equipment, stop if unwell.

los.text: Define the clinical indications for using PEFR and spirometry in assessing respiratory function and disease.
los.html:
PEFR indications
  • Asthma diagnosis (variability >20% over 2 weeks) and monitoring (self-management, action plans: personal best zones)
  • Acute asthma severity (% predicted/best guides treatment)
  • Occupational asthma (serial PEF at work vs home, OASYS)
  • Assess response to treatment.
  • Effort-dependent
  • Less useful in COPD.
Spirometry indications
  • Diagnosis: asthma (with BDR), COPD (required for diagnosis: post-BD FEV1/FVC <0.7), restrictive lung disease (ILD, neuromuscular, chest wall, obesity).
  • Severity and monitoring: COPD grading (GOLD FEV1 %), ILD progression, CF, neuromuscular disease (FVC in GBS/MND: lying vs standing for diaphragm weakness).
  • Pre-operative assessment (lung resection), occupational screening, drug toxicity monitoring (amiodarone, methotrexate, bleomycin), research.
Further testsFull lung function (lung volumes: TLC, RV by body plethysmography/helium dilution; TLCO/KCO gas transfer: ↓ in emphysema, ILD, PE/pulmonary hypertension, anaemia; ↑ in pulmonary haemorrhage, asthma), FeNO, bronchial challenge.

los.text: Analyse and interpret PEFR and spirometry readings, identify common respiratory patterns, and use this information to formulate potential diagnoses.
los.html:
PatternFEV1FVCFEV1/FVCCauses
Obstructive↓↓Normal/↓<0.7 (or <LLN)Asthma (reversible: ↑ FEV1 ≥12% + 200 mL), COPD (largely irreversible), bronchiectasis, CF, bronchiolitis obliterans
Restrictive↓↓↓Normal or ↑ (>0.7)ILD/pulmonary fibrosis, chest wall (kyphoscoliosis, obesity), neuromuscular (MND, myasthenia, GBS, diaphragm palsy), pleural thickening, post-pneumonectomy
Mixed↓↓<0.7Combined disease (e.g. COPD + fibrosis, CF)
Flow–volume loop
  • Obstructive → "scooped"/concave expiratory limb
  • Restrictive → small, narrow but normal-shaped loop
  • Upper airway obstruction → flattened inspiratory (variable extrathoracic) or both limbs (fixed: tracheal stenosis).
COPD severity (GOLD, FEV1 % predicted)Mild ≥80, moderate 50–79, severe 30–49, very severe <30.
PEFDiurnal variability >20% suggests asthma; low PEF falling at work = occupational asthma.
NoteRestriction confirmed by ↓ TLC on lung volumes; TLCO distinguishes parenchymal (↓) from extraparenchymal (normal KCO) restriction.
PitfallsPoor technique/effort; fixed 0.7 ratio overdiagnoses obstruction in elderly (use LLN/z-scores, GLI equations).

los.text: Recognise common radiographic features of acute respiratory presentations, including pulmonary oedema, pneumothorax, pleural effusion, consolidation, and lung masses
los.html:
ConditionCXR features
Pulmonary oedema
  • ABCDE: Alveolar oedema (bat's-wing perihilar shadowing)
  • Kerley B lines (interstitial oedema)
  • Cardiomegaly (CTR >0.5 on PA)
  • Dilated upper lobe vessels (upper lobe diversion)
  • Pleural Effusions (+ fluid in horizontal fissure)
PneumothoraxVisible visceral pleural edge with no lung markings beyond; deep sulcus sign (supine); tension: mediastinal shift away, flattened hemidiaphragm
Pleural effusionBlunting of costophrenic angle, homogeneous opacity with meniscus (curved upper edge), large → mediastinal shift away; supine: hazy hemithorax
Consolidation
  • Airspace opacification
  • Air bronchograms
  • Loss of adjacent borders (silhouette sign: RML → right heart border; lingula → left heart border; lower lobes → hemidiaphragm)
  • No volume loss
Lung massRounded opacity (>3 cm = mass, <3 cm nodule), spiculated edges, cavitation (SCC, abscess, TB), hilar enlargement, collapse, effusion, rib destruction
CollapseVolume loss → shift towards, raised hemidiaphragm; LLL collapse: "sail sign" behind heart; RUL: elevated horizontal fissure

los.text: Differentiate between key causes of shortness of breath and chest pain on chest X-ray, such as infection, heart failure, trauma, and malignancy
los.html:
PresentationCXR clues
Infection (pneumonia)Focal consolidation ± air bronchograms, parapneumonic effusion, cavitation (S. aureus, Klebsiella, TB: upper lobe)
Heart failureCardiomegaly, upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, bat's wing oedema, bilateral effusions
Trauma
  • Rib fractures (flail segment)
  • Pneumothorax
  • Haemothorax (effusion)
  • Surgical emphysema
  • Pulmonary contusion (patchy opacity)
  • Widened mediastinum (aortic injury)
  • Diaphragmatic rupture (bowel in chest)
  • Clavicle/scapula fractures
MalignancyMass, hilar lymphadenopathy, collapse, unilateral effusion, bony metastases, raised hemidiaphragm (phrenic palsy)
PEOften normal (helps exclude others); occasionally wedge-shaped infarct, Westermark sign (oligaemia), small effusion
Aortic dissectionWidened mediastinum (>8 cm), abnormal aortic knuckle
Pneumothorax / COPD / asthmaHyperinflation (>6 anterior ribs/>10 posterior), flat diaphragms, bullae
Pericardial effusionLarge globular "flask-shaped" heart
Perforated viscus (chest pain/abdominal)Free air under the diaphragm on erect CXR
  • Remember: a normal CXR doesn't exclude ACS, PE, early pneumonia or small pneumothorax.

los.text: Interpret chest X-rays systematically, identifying abnormalities such as mediastinal shift, air–fluid levels, and surgical emphysema
los.html:
Systematic approach
  • Details: name, date, previous films; projection (PA vs AP: AP magnifies heart), erect/supine.
  • Quality (RIPE): Rotation (spinous processes midway between clavicle heads), Inspiration (5–6 anterior ribs or 10 posterior), Projection, Exposure (vertebrae just visible behind heart).
  • ABCDE: Airway (trachea central? carina, bronchi), Breathing (lung fields in zones, compare sides; pleura, costophrenic angles, pneumothorax), Circulation (heart size: CTR <0.5 PA, borders, mediastinum width, hila), Diaphragm (right higher than left, free air underneath, gastric bubble), Everything else (bones: ribs, clavicles, spine; soft tissues: surgical emphysema, breast shadows; lines and tubes: ETT, NG tube, central lines, chest drains, pacemakers).
  • Review areas: apices, behind heart, hila, below diaphragms, costophrenic angles.
Specific abnormalities
  • Mediastinal shift: away from tension pneumothorax/large effusion/mass; towards collapse/pneumonectomy/fibrosis.
  • Air–fluid levels: hydropneumothorax (horizontal line in pleural space), lung abscess (cavity with fluid level), hiatus hernia (behind heart), oesophageal obstruction.
  • Surgical emphysema: dark streaks of gas in soft tissues of chest wall/neck (pneumothorax, chest drain, oesophageal rupture, trauma).
ReportDescribe → interpret → summarise → suggest next step.

los.text: Apply the principle of “old is gold” by comparing current and previous imaging to aid diagnosis and avoid unnecessary investigations
los.html:
"Old is gold"Always compare with previous imaging before acting.
Benefits
  • Distinguish new vs chronic abnormalities: e.g. stable nodule for years (benign), chronic pleural thickening or old fractures, long-standing cardiomegaly, chronic changes of bronchiectasis/fibrosis, post-surgical changes.
  • Assess progression or resolution (pneumonia resolving at 6 weeks, effusion increasing, mass enlarging → cancer workup).
  • Avoid unnecessary investigations (CT for an unchanged lesion), radiation exposure, cost, patient anxiety.
  • Helps interpret subtle findings (e.g. new small effusion vs baseline).
Practice
  • Check PACS for prior images (and previous reports) from other hospitals (Welsh Imaging Archive), note dates
  • Documentation: "compared with CXR dated ..., there is new ...".
Fleischner/BTS nodule guidanceSolid nodule stable for 2 years on CT is usually considered benign (volumetry; ground-glass needs longer follow-up).

los.text: Explain the clinical significance of findings (e.g., tension vs simple pneumothorax, pulmonary oedema vs infection) and suggest appropriate next steps in management or further investigation
los.html:
Simple vs tension pneumothorax
  • Simple: air in pleural space without haemodynamic compromise; CXR: pleural line, no markings. Mx: conservative/aspiration/drain by size and symptoms (BTS 2023).
  • Tension: one-way valve → progressive ↑ intrathoracic pressure → mediastinal shift away, ↓ venous return → hypotension, tachycardia, ↑ JVP, hypoxia, tracheal deviation (late). Clinical diagnosis → immediate needle/finger thoracostomy (don't wait for CXR) then chest drain. If CXR obtained: large pneumothorax, mediastinal shift, depressed hemidiaphragm, widened rib spaces.
Pulmonary oedema vs infection
  • Oedema: bilateral, perihilar/symmetrical, Kerley B lines, upper lobe diversion, cardiomegaly, effusions; clinical: orthopnoea, PND, ↑ JVP, oedema, ↑ NT-proBNP → IV furosemide, nitrates, sit up, O₂, CPAP, treat cause (ACS, AF).
  • Infection: focal/lobar consolidation, air bronchograms, fever, ↑ CRP/WCC, productive cough → antibiotics (CURB-65), cultures.
  • Can coexist; ARDS/COVID: bilateral peripheral opacities without cardiomegaly.
EffusionUnilateral → diagnostic tap (USS-guided); bilateral with HF → treat HF first.
MassCT chest/abdomen with contrast → 2WW lung cancer pathway.
Next stepsFurther imaging (CT, USS, CTPA), bloods, ABG, specialist referral, treatment.

los.text: Evaluate when imaging findings represent urgent, life-threatening conditions that require immediate intervention (e.g., tension pneumothorax, flail chest, massive effusion)
los.html:
Immediately life-threatening findings (treat now, often before imaging)
  • Tension pneumothorax → needle/finger decompression.
  • Massive haemothorax (>1.5 L or ongoing) → chest drain, transfusion, thoracotomy if >200 mL/h.
  • Flail chest (≥2 fractures in ≥3 adjacent ribs → paradoxical movement) + underlying pulmonary contusion → analgesia (regional blocks), O₂, ventilation, rib fixation.
  • Open pneumothorax ("sucking chest wound") → vented occlusive dressing + chest drain.
  • Cardiac tamponade (globular heart, ↑ JVP, hypotension, muffled sounds) → pericardiocentesis/thoracotomy.
  • Massive pleural effusion with mediastinal shift and respiratory compromise → urgent therapeutic drainage (slowly; re-expansion oedema).
  • Widened mediastinum after deceleration trauma → aortic injury → CT angiography.
  • Free air under the diaphragm → perforated viscus → surgical review.
  • Large/central lung mass with SVC obstruction or airway compromise, misplaced tubes (ETT in right main bronchus, NG tube in lung → don't feed).
Action
  • Recognise → escalate immediately to senior/relevant team → ABCDE resuscitation → definitive intervention
  • Communicate urgent findings directly (radiology "critical findings" pathway).

los.text: Develop a problem-solving approach by integrating clinical information (such as symptoms, history, and risk factors) with radiographic findings
los.html:
Clinical–radiological integrationInterpret imaging in context of age, symptoms, timeline, risk factors and examination.
Approach
1. Pre-test probabilityWhat do history and exam suggest? (e.g. 70-year-old smoker with haemoptysis and weight loss → malignancy).
2Request appropriate imaging with clear clinical question (better reports).
3Systematic read (avoid satisfaction of search: keep looking after first finding).
4. CorrelateDoes the finding explain the symptoms? (e.g. consolidation + fever = pneumonia; effusion + heart failure signs; normal CXR + pleuritic pain + tachycardia → PE).
5Generate differentials and decide next test (CT, USS, bloods, bronchoscopy) or treatment.
6Compare old films, review response to treatment, follow-up imaging (6-week CXR after pneumonia in smokers/>50).
Examples
  • Young tall man with sudden pleuritic pain → pneumothorax
  • Elderly with confusion and RLL consolidation → aspiration pneumonia
  • Post-op day 5 breathless with clear CXR → PE
  • Asbestos worker with unilateral effusion + pleural thickening → mesothelioma.
Cognitive pitfallsAnchoring, premature closure, framing; avoid over-reliance on imaging alone.

los.text: Demonstrate the major features and boundaries of the oral cavity and summarise its sensory innervation
los.html:
Boundaries of the oral cavity
  • Anterior: lips (oral fissure)
  • Lateral: cheeks (buccinator)
  • Roof: hard palate (maxilla palatine processes + palatine bones) and soft palate
  • Floor: mylohyoid (oral diaphragm) + geniohyoid, tongue
  • Posterior: oropharyngeal isthmus (palatoglossal folds).
  • Divided into vestibule (between lips/cheeks and teeth) and oral cavity proper.
Features
  • Teeth and gums
  • Tongue
  • Palate
  • Uvula
  • Palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches (tonsils between)
  • Frenulum
  • Sublingual papillae/folds (submandibular/sublingual duct openings)
  • Parotid papilla (opposite upper 2nd molar).
Sensory innervation(mainly trigeminal)
  • Upper lip, upper teeth/gums, hard palate: maxillary nerve (V2): superior alveolar nerves, greater palatine (hard palate), nasopalatine (anterior palate), lesser palatine (soft palate).
  • Lower lip, chin, lower teeth/gums: mandibular nerve (V3): inferior alveolar → mental nerve; buccal nerve (cheek mucosa).
  • Floor of mouth and anterior ⅔ tongue: lingual nerve (V3).
  • Posterior ⅓ tongue, oropharynx, tonsils: glossopharyngeal (IX) (gag reflex afferent); vagus (X) near epiglottis.

los.text: Identify the parotid, submandibular and sublingual salivary glands, and their locations in the living, the courses of their ducts into the oral cavity, their autonomic secretomotor innervation, lymph drainage routes, and their secretions.
los.html:
GlandLocationDuctSecretomotor (parasympathetic)Lymph drainageSecretion
Parotid (largest)
  • In front of and below ear, over masseter, wraps around ramus
  • Enclosed in parotid fascia (from investing layer; tense → painful swelling in mumps)
Stensen's (parotid) duct: crosses masseter, pierces buccinator, opens opposite upper 2nd molarIX → tympanic nerve → lesser petrosal → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve (V3)Parotid (pre-auricular) → deep cervical nodesSerous (watery, amylase)
SubmandibularSubmandibular triangle; superficial part wraps around posterior border of mylohyoid into deep partWharton's duct: runs forward in floor of mouth (crossed by lingual nerve), opens at sublingual papilla beside frenulumVII → chorda tympani → (with lingual nerve) → submandibular ganglionSubmandibular → deep cervicalMixed (mainly serous)
Sublingual (smallest)Floor of mouth under sublingual fold, above mylohyoidMultiple small ducts (Rivinus) onto sublingual fold ± Bartholin's duct into submandibular ductVII via submandibular ganglionSubmandibular, submentalMainly mucous
Sympathetic(superior cervical ganglion, along arteries)Thick, viscous, scanty saliva; parasympathetic → copious watery saliva.
Palpation in the livingParotid (anterior to ear, hard to feel unless enlarged); submandibular bimanual palpation (finger in floor of mouth + external hand).

los.text: Appreciate the narrow points of the ducts in relation to salivary stone impaction.
los.html:
Salivary stones (sialolithiasis)
  • ~80–90% in the submandibular gland. Why:
  • Saliva more viscous/mucous and alkaline, with higher Ca²⁺.
  • Duct is long and runs uphill (against gravity).
  • Sharp bend around the posterior border of mylohyoid.
Narrow points where stones impact
  • Submandibular duct: at the hilum of the gland/bend around posterior mylohyoid and at the ostium/sublingual papilla (narrowest point).
  • Parotid duct: where it turns medially around the anterior border of masseter and pierces buccinator, and at the ostium.
PresentationMeal-time pain and swelling (salivary colic), resolving after; recurrent infection (sialadenitis: pus from duct).
Ix/Mx
  • USS (or sialography/CT)
  • Hydration, massage, sialogogues (lemon drops)
  • Stone removal (via duct incision: beware lingual nerve in floor of mouth), sialendoscopy, gland excision.

los.text: List the structures within the parotid gland.
los.html:
Structures within the parotid gland (superficial → deep)
  • Facial nerve (CN VII) and its branches: enters posteromedially from stylomastoid foramen, divides within the gland at the pes anserinus into 5 terminal branches: Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal mandibular, Cervical ("To Zanzibar By Motor Car"). The nerve separates superficial and deep lobes (surgical plane).
  • Retromandibular vein (formed by superficial temporal + maxillary veins).
  • External carotid artery (deepest), dividing into superficial temporal and maxillary arteries within the gland.
  • Parotid lymph nodes.
  • Branches of auriculotemporal nerve (secretomotor fibres).
Clinical
  • Parotid tumours (pleomorphic adenoma: commonest, benign; Warthin's tumour: smokers, bilateral) → facial nerve palsy suggests malignancy
  • Parotidectomy risks facial nerve injury and Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating: auriculotemporal fibres regrow into sweat glands)
  • Mumps, sialadenitis.

los.text: Describe the structure of the tongue including the papillae.
los.html:
DivisionsAnterior ⅔ (oral part) and posterior ⅓ (pharyngeal part) separated by sulcus terminalis (V-shaped) with foramen caecum at apex (origin of thyroglossal duct).
Dorsum anterior ⅔ papillae
  • Filiform: most numerous, rough texture, no taste buds (mechanical, keratinised).
  • Fungiform: mushroom-shaped, scattered (tip/sides), red dots, have taste buds.
  • Circumvallate (vallate): 8–12 large papillae in a V just in front of sulcus terminalis, surrounded by trench, many taste buds; von Ebner's serous glands.
  • Foliate: folds on lateral margins posteriorly, taste buds (prominent in children).
Posterior ⅓No papillae; lingual tonsil (lymphoid nodules) → bumpy surface.
Inferior surfaceThin mucosa, frenulum, deep lingual veins (visible; sublingual GTN absorption), fimbriated folds.
MuscleSkeletal muscle in interlacing bundles divided by midline lingual septum.
Blood supply
  • Lingual artery (external carotid)
  • Venous drainage to IJV.
  • Lymph: tip → submental nodes
  • Anterior ⅔ → submandibular
  • Posterior ⅓ → deep cervical (bilateral drainage near midline → tongue cancer can spread bilaterally).

los.text: List the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue, describing their attachments and innervations.
los.html:
Intrinsic muscles(within tongue; no bony attachment; change shape)Superior longitudinal (shortens, curls tip up), inferior longitudinal (shortens, curls tip down), transverse (narrows and elongates), vertical (flattens and broadens).
Extrinsic muscles(attach to bone; change position)
MuscleAttachmentsAction
GenioglossusSuperior mental spine of mandible → tongue dorsum, hyoidProtrudes tongue (and depresses centre); prevents tongue falling back (airway; jaw thrust)
HyoglossusHyoid (body, greater horn) → side of tongueDepresses and retracts
StyloglossusStyloid process → side of tongueRetracts and elevates (swallowing)
PalatoglossusPalatine aponeurosis → side of tongueElevates posterior tongue, closes oropharyngeal isthmus
  • Innervation: all intrinsic and extrinsic muscles by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) except palatoglossus (vagus, CN X, via pharyngeal plexus).

los.text: Explain the sensory innervation (general and taste sensation) of the tongue.
los.html:
RegionGeneral sensationTaste
Anterior ⅔Lingual nerve (V3, mandibular)
  • Chorda tympani (VII): fibres run in the lingual nerve at first, then leave it as the chorda tympani
  • → middle ear
  • → facial nerve (cell bodies in the geniculate ganglion)
  • → nucleus of solitary tract
Posterior ⅓ (+ circumvallate papillae)Glossopharyngeal (IX)Glossopharyngeal (IX)
Root/epiglottic regionInternal laryngeal nerve (X)Vagus (X)
PathwayTaste fibres → nucleus of the tractus solitarius (gustatory part, medulla) → VPM thalamus → gustatory cortex (insula/frontal operculum).
Clinical
  • Bell's palsy proximal to chorda tympani → loss of taste anterior ⅔
  • Lingual nerve injury (third molar extraction, submandibular surgery) → numbness and taste loss anterior ⅔ (chorda fibres travel with it)
  • Glossopharyngeal lesions → loss of gag reflex (afferent) and taste posterior ⅓.

los.text: Explain the deviation of the tongue after hypoglossal nerve injuries.
los.html:
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies the intrinsic muscles and genioglossus on the same side.
LMN lesion(nerve itself: trauma, neck surgery (carotid endarterectomy, submandibular gland excision), skull base tumours, dissection)
  • Ipsilateral weakness of genioglossus → on protrusion, the tongue deviates towards the side of the lesion (unopposed action of the normal genioglossus pushes it over)
  • Ipsilateral wasting and fasciculations of tongue.
UMN lesion(e.g. stroke affecting corticobulbar fibres)
  • Tongue deviates away from the side of the cortical lesion (towards the weak side, i.e. contralateral), no wasting
  • Often mild because most hypoglossal nuclei receive bilateral input (except genioglossus, mainly contralateral).
Bilateral lesionsBulbar palsy (LMN: MND, wasted fasciculating tongue) vs pseudobulbar palsy (UMN: small spastic tongue, brisk jaw jerk, emotional lability).
Mnemonic"Lick your wounds": the tongue points towards the damaged nerve.

los.text: Describe the otic ganglion.
los.html:
Otic ganglion
  • Small parasympathetic ganglion in the infratemporal fossa
  • Just below the foramen ovale
  • Medial to the mandibular nerve (V3)
  • Lateral to tensor veli palatini.
Roots
  • Parasympathetic (motor) root: preganglionic fibres from inferior salivatory nucleus → glossopharyngeal (IX) → tympanic nerve (Jacobson's) → tympanic plexus (middle ear) → lesser petrosal nerve → through foramen ovale → synapse in otic ganglion.
  • Sympathetic root: postganglionic fibres from superior cervical ganglion via plexus on middle meningeal artery (pass through without synapsing).
  • Sensory/motor fibres from V3 pass through (nerve to medial pterygoid → tensor veli palatini and tensor tympani).
DistributionPostganglionic parasympathetic fibres join the auriculotemporal nerve (V3) → parotid gland (secretomotor).
Clinical
  • Frey's syndrome after parotid surgery (aberrant regeneration of these fibres to sweat glands)
  • The pathway explains why IX lesions reduce parotid secretion.
